metadata.title: Liver Histology: The Hepatic Lobule
metadata.subject: Histology & Pathology
metadata.description: Trace blood and bile through the classical hepatic lobule, then connect microscopic landmarks to their functional zones and characteristic patterns of injury.
metadata.author: Medical Sciences Faculty

nodes.text: At low magnification, the classical hepatic lobule is organized around a
central vein
. Plates of hepatocytes and intervening sinusoids radiate toward it. The geometric boundary is subtle in human liver, so use vascular landmarks rather than expecting a sharply outlined hexagon.
At the lobular periphery, locate a
portal tract
. Several portal tracts surround each central venous outflow region, creating the structural basis for gradients of oxygenation and substrate exposure.
Within the connective tissue of the portal tract, compare the thin-walled, relatively wide
portal venule
with the smaller, rounder
hepatic arteriole
. The arteriole has a conspicuous muscular wall relative to its lumen.
The
interlobular bile duct
is lined by cuboidal cholangiocytes. Unlike the adjacent vessels, it usually maintains a crisp epithelial boundary and contains no erythrocytes.
Portal venous and hepatic arterial blood mix in the
hepatic sinusoids
and flows centripetally toward the central vein. Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelial cells permit exchange with the perisinusoidal space of Disse.
A
Kupffer cell
lies along the luminal face of the sinusoid and participates in phagocytosis. Do not confuse its elongated or irregular nucleus with the flatter nucleus of a sinusoidal endothelial cell.

sections.title: Integrate opposing flows and metabolic zones

nodes.text: Blood flows portal tract → central vein; bile flows in the opposite direction.
Canaliculi between adjacent hepatocytes conduct bile toward canals of Hering and portal bile ductules.
The periportal region,
acinus zone 1
, receives oxygenated blood first. The centrilobular region,
acinus zone 3
, is relatively hypoxic and has high CYP450 activity. This helps explain why ischemia and several toxic injuries preferentially affect zone 3.
